speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I work from home, can I deduct part of my rent and utilities?

**Jordan:** It depends on where you file and whether you’re an employee or self-employed. For U.S. federal taxes, employees generally can’t deduct unreimbursed home-office expenses. Self-employed people may qualify if they use a specific area **regularly and exclusively** for business and it meets a business-use test, such as being their principal place of business.

**Alex:** Does it have to be a separate room?

**Jordan:** No. A dedicated part of a room can qualify, but a kitchen table you also use for meals generally won’t. There are exceptions to the exclusive-use rule for qualifying daycare and certain inventory storage.

**Alex:** How do I calculate the deduction if I qualify?

**Jordan:** You can generally choose between two methods. The **simplified method** is $5 per square foot, up to 300 square feet, for a maximum of $1,500, subject to income limits. The **actual-expense method** generally lets you deduct the business share of eligible costs like rent, utilities, and insurance. If you own your home, that method can also involve depreciation, which may affect your taxes when you sell.

**Alex:** So I should compare both methods rather than assume the simpler one saves more?

**Jordan:** Exactly. Keep a record of the workspace’s size and, if you’re considering the actual-expense method, your bills and receipts. If you’re an employee, ask whether your employer reimburses eligible expenses; also check your state’s rules, which can differ from federal rules.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can you show me how the two methods compare?

**Jordan:** Say you’re self-employed and use 150 square feet of a 1,000-square-foot apartment exclusively and regularly for business. The simplified method gives you a $750 deduction. If you paid $18,000 in eligible rent and utilities for the year, the actual-expense method would generally allocate 15% of those costs to the office, or $2,700, before any applicable limits.

**Alex:** Does that mean I’d save $2,700 on my taxes?

**Jordan:** No. A deduction reduces the income you’re taxed on; it doesn’t reduce your tax bill dollar for dollar. Also, if the business-income limit prevents you from taking the full deduction, some expenses under the actual-expense method may carry forward. An unused simplified deduction doesn’t. You can generally choose the method anew each year.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** So how much would the $2,700 deduction actually save me?

**Jordan:** If you can take the full deduction and each dollar offsets income in the 22% federal bracket, it would save about **$594 in federal income tax**, compared with **$165** for the $750 simplified deduction. That’s **$429 more** with the actual-expense method in this example. The deduction may also affect self-employment and state taxes, so those figures aren’t a full estimate.

**Alex:** What would I need to claim the actual expenses?

**Jordan:** Keep your lease, utility bills, and a record of how you measured the office and apartment. If you’re a sole proprietor filing Schedule C, you’d generally use **Form 8829** for actual expenses. With the simplified method, you generally use the worksheet in the Schedule C instructions instead.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Do I send all those records to the IRS with my return?

**Jordan:** Generally, no. If you’re a sole proprietor using the actual-expense method, you normally file Form 8829 with your return and keep the supporting records in case the IRS asks for them.

**Alex:** Do I apply the 15% to every bill?

**Jordan:** No. Apply it to eligible costs for the whole apartment, like rent and utilities. A repair that benefits only the office, such as repainting just that area, is generally a direct expense and isn’t prorated, though the overall deduction limit still applies. A repair that benefits only a personal area, like your bedroom, doesn’t count.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I only used the office for part of the year?

**Jordan:** With the actual-expense method, count only expenses for the period when the office qualified. If you started using it on July 1 and paid $9,000 in eligible rent and utilities from July through December, you’d apply the 15% to that $9,000. That’s a **$1,350 deduction** before any applicable limits.

**Alex:** And with the simplified method?

**Jordan:** You’d use your average qualifying square footage for the year. In this example, 150 square feet for six months averages out to 75 square feet over 12 months. At $5 per square foot, that’s **$375**, before the business-income limit. If you start or stop midmonth, a month counts only if you had at least 15 days of qualifying use.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I move during the year and set up a qualifying office in my new apartment, can I use the simplified method for both?

**Jordan:** Not for both. For U.S. federal taxes, you can use the simplified method for only **one home per year**. If both offices qualify, you can use the simplified method for one home and actual expenses for the other, or use actual expenses for both.

**Alex:** What records should I keep for the move?

**Jordan:** Note when each office started and stopped qualifying, and measure each workspace separately. For any home where you use actual expenses, keep its bills separate and use that home’s business-use percentage. The 15% from your old apartment doesn’t automatically carry over to the new one.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How do I decide which apartment to use the simplified method for?

**Jordan:** Compare the combined deduction three ways: actual expenses for both homes, simplified for the old home and actual for the new one, and actual for the old home and simplified for the new one.

**Alex:** Can we use the numbers from earlier?

**Jordan:** Sure. Say the old office qualified from January through June, with the same 150 square feet and $9,000 in eligible expenses we discussed. That’s **$1,350 using actual expenses** or **$375 using the simplified method**. Now say the new office qualified from July through December, measured 200 square feet, and had $400 in eligible expenses *after* applying its own business-use percentage. The simplified deduction for the new office would be **$500**.

| Method | Combined deduction before applicable limits |
|---|---:|
| Actual for both homes | $1,750 |
| Simplified for old, actual for new | $775 |
| Actual for old, simplified for new | **$1,850** |

**Alex:** So I don’t have to pick one method for the whole year?

**Jordan:** Right. In this example, actual expenses work better for the old apartment and the simplified method works better for the new one. Check the applicable business-income limits before deciding how much you can claim.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I go with the $1,850 option, how do I report it?

**Jordan:** If you’re a sole proprietor and both offices were for the same Schedule C business, use **Form 8829** to calculate the actual-expense deduction for the old apartment. Use the **simplified-method worksheet** in the Schedule C instructions for the new apartment. Add the allowable amounts and report the total on **Schedule C, line 30**. Keep the worksheet and your records showing when each office qualified.

**Alex:** What if the income limit cuts the deduction?

**Jordan:** The $1,850 is the amount before the limits. Eligible actual expenses you can’t deduct may carry forward to a later year when you use the actual-expense method. Any portion of the simplified deduction you can’t use is lost.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I have $1,600 of business profit left before the home-office deduction, can I claim $1,600 of the $1,850?

**Jordan:** Not necessarily. When you move and use two qualifying homes, you generally allocate the business income and expenses between them based on the time you used each home for business. Then you apply the deduction limit separately to each home.

**Alex:** What would that look like in our example?

**Jordan:** Suppose the allocation leaves an $800 limit for each apartment. You’d deduct **$800** of the old apartment’s $1,350 in actual expenses and the full **$500** simplified deduction for the new apartment. That’s **$1,300 on Schedule C, line 30**. The new apartment’s unused $300 of limit can’t absorb the old apartment’s expenses, but the old apartment’s remaining **$550** may carry forward, subject to the actual-expense rules.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I use the simplified method next year, do I lose that $550 carryforward?

**Jordan:** No. You can’t deduct the carryforward in a year you use the simplified method, but you can generally save it for a later year when you use the actual-expense method, subject to that year’s deduction limit.

**Alex:** What should I keep to track it?

**Jordan:** Keep the old apartment’s Form 8829 and a note showing how much carried forward and in which expense categories. That way, you’ll have the figures you need when you next use the actual-expense method.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Since I moved, can I use the old apartment’s $550 carryforward at the new apartment?

**Jordan:** Generally, yes. Moving doesn’t by itself erase the carryforward. If you continue the same business and use the actual-expense method for a qualifying home office in a later year, you can generally include the $550 on that year’s Form 8829, subject to the deduction limit.

**Alex:** And if I use the simplified method for another year?

**Jordan:** Leave the $550 off that year’s deduction and keep tracking it. The simplified method doesn’t let you claim prior actual expenses, but it doesn’t wipe them out either.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Does that mean I should switch to actual expenses next year just to use the $550?

**Jordan:** Not necessarily. Compare the **allowable actual-expense deduction, including any usable carryforward**, with the simplified deduction. For example, if your new office qualifies at 200 square feet for all 12 months, the simplified deduction would be **$1,000**. If your current-year actual expenses come to **$400 after applying the business-use percentage**, adding the $550 carryforward would bring the actual-expense deduction to **$950** before applicable limits. If you can take either deduction in full, the simplified method gives you $50 more that year, and you can still keep the $550 carryforward for a future year when you use actual expenses.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if my actual expenses go up next year?

**Jordan:** In this example, **$450 in current-year deductible office expenses** is the break-even point: add the $550 carryforward and you match the $1,000 simplified deduction. If your expenses rise to $600 after applying the business-use percentage, the actual-expense method could give you a **$1,150 deduction**, assuming the income limit lets you take it all.

**Alex:** So I don’t need to decide now?

**Jordan:** Right. Keep the bills and the carryforward record, then compare the deductions you can actually claim when you prepare your return. There’s no need to switch methods just to use the $550.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can I see the $600 example side by side?

**Jordan:** Sure. If your 200-square-foot office qualifies all year and the income limit doesn’t reduce either deduction:

| Method | Deduction next year | Carryforward remaining |
|---|---:|---:|
| Actual expenses: $600 plus the $550 carryforward | $1,150 | $0 |
| Simplified: 200 square feet × $5 | $1,000 | $550 |

**Alex:** So actual expenses give me $150 more now, but simplified keeps the $550 available?

**Jordan:** Exactly. That’s **$150 more in deductions**, not $150 off your tax bill. If you choose simplified, the $550 stays available for a later year when you use actual expenses, subject to that year’s deduction limit.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I expect to use the $550 later, could the simplified method be the better choice?

**Jordan:** Yes. In this example, the simplified method gives up **$150 in deductions now** but preserves a **potential $550 deduction later**. The key is whether you’ll have a qualifying home office, use the actual-expense method, and have enough business income to deduct the carryforward.

**Alex:** What if I’m not sure I’ll qualify later?

**Jordan:** Then taking the **$1,150 actual-expense deduction now** may make more sense. Compare the tax savings you can claim now with what you realistically expect to save later, especially if your tax rate might change.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** How would I put a dollar value on that trade-off?

**Jordan:** Using the same 22% federal income tax rate, the extra **$150 deduction** under the actual-expense method saves about **$33 now**. If you choose the simplified method and later use the full **$550 carryforward** at that same rate, it could save about **$121 later**. That comparison assumes the carryforward adds to a deduction you’d otherwise take; if you’d have to switch to a less favorable method just to use it, the benefit could be smaller.

**Alex:** So what’s the practical call?

**Jordan:** If you expect to qualify and use actual expenses again soon, keeping the carryforward may be worth giving up $33 today. If you’re likely to stop qualifying or stick with the simplified method, taking the larger deduction now may be the better choice.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How sure would I need to be that I’ll use the carryforward?

**Jordan:** In our example, the break-even chance is about **27%**: $33 in tax savings now divided by $121 in potential tax savings later. That assumes you either use the full $550 as an *additional* deduction or get no benefit from it, your federal marginal rate stays at 22%, and you don’t discount the future savings.

**Alex:** What if I expect to use only part of it?

**Jordan:** Compare the **extra deduction you realistically expect to get later** with the $150 extra deduction you can take now. At the same tax rate, if only $100 would actually increase your future deduction, that’s $22 in federal income tax savings—not enough to give up $33 today. And the longer you expect to wait, the more valuable the immediate savings become by comparison.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I have a 50% chance of getting an extra $300 deduction next year?

**Jordan:** At a 22% federal marginal rate, that’s a 50% chance of saving $66, or **$33 in expected tax savings**. That ties the $33 you could save now with actual expenses, before accounting for the wait. If you’d rather have a sure $33 today than a chance at $66 next year, choose actual expenses.

**Alex:** What counts as an “extra” deduction?

**Jordan:** Compare what you’d actually claim next year **with and without** the carryforward, choosing the better method in each case. Suppose next year’s simplified deduction is $1,000 and actual expenses would be $750 without the carryforward or $1,300 with it, after applicable limits. The carryforward increases your best deduction by **$300**, not $550, because you could already deduct $1,000 using the simplified method.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** In the other 50% of cases, what if I don’t use the carryforward next year but can still use it later?

**Jordan:** Then $33 is the expected tax savings **next year**, not the full value of keeping the carryforward. To compare it with the sure $33 today, also count any additional tax savings you realistically expect in later years, adjusted for the chance you’ll get them and how long you’ll wait.

**Alex:** In the $1,300 example, do I still have $250 to carry forward because only $300 helped me?

**Jordan:** No. If you deduct $750 in current expenses plus the full $550 carryforward, you’ve used all $550. The **$300** is how much better that result is than the $1,000 simplified deduction. What you use up on your return and what you gain by choosing that method are two different numbers.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** When would I actually have $250 left to carry forward?

**Jordan:** Suppose you have $750 in current-year actual expenses, but the income limit lets you deduct only $1,050 in total. If $300 of the $550 carryforward fits under that limit, you’d deduct $1,050 and keep the remaining **$250** for a later year, subject to the applicable limits.

**Alex:** And if I could still deduct $1,000 using the simplified method?

**Jordan:** Then actual expenses would give you just **$50 more in deductions now** and leave you with $250 to carry forward. Choosing simplified would give you the $1,000 deduction and preserve the full $550. So the trade-off is whether using $300 of the carryforward is worth the tax savings on an extra $50 deduction today.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** At a 22% tax rate, what’s that trade-off worth?

**Jordan:** The $50 larger deduction saves **$11 in federal income tax now**. Choosing the simplified method preserves an extra **$300 of carryforward** ($550 instead of $250). If all $300 later increases the deduction you’d otherwise claim, it could save **$66** at the same tax rate.

**Alex:** How likely would that future savings need to be?

**Jordan:** If the extra $300 either saves you the full $66 or saves you nothing, the break-even chance is about **17%** ($11 ÷ $66), ignoring the wait. The key is to value only what that extra $300 adds: if the $250 you’d retain under either method already fills your future deduction limit, preserving more won’t help in that year.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I can use $100 of that extra $300 next year and the other $200 later?

**Jordan:** Value each portion separately. At a 22% federal marginal rate, the first $100 could save **$22 next year**, and the remaining $200 could save **$44 later**—but only to the extent each portion increases the deduction you’d otherwise claim. Adjust each amount for the chance you’ll actually get that savings and for how long you’ll wait, then compare the total with the **$11 you can save now**.

**Alex:** So if I’m confident the first $100 will increase next year’s deduction, I don’t need to count on the rest?

**Jordan:** Right. In this example, **$22 next year versus $11 today** would generally favor the simplified method even if the remaining $200 never helps.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How confident do I need to be if I ignore the remaining $200?

**Jordan:** At the same 22% federal marginal rate, the break-even chance is **50%** before accounting for the wait: a 50% chance of saving $22 next year is worth $11 in expected savings. Since the $11 is available today, you’d need a slightly higher chance to favor the simplified method on that $100 alone.

**Alex:** And that $100 has to be on top of what I’d otherwise deduct?

**Jordan:** Exactly. Compare next year’s best allowable deduction with **$550 carried forward** against what you could claim with **$250 carried forward**. If the larger carryforward raises that deduction by $100, the $22 savings is real. If both balances lead to the same deduction next year, there’s no extra savings that year.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can you show me how the extra carryforward could add just $100?

**Jordan:** Suppose next year you have $850 in current-year actual expenses, a $1,200 deduction limit, and a $1,000 simplified deduction. With **$250 carried forward**, you could deduct **$1,100** using actual expenses. With **$550 carried forward**, you’d hit the **$1,200 limit** and have $200 left to carry forward. Actual expenses beat the simplified method in both cases, so the larger carryforward adds exactly **$100 to next year’s deduction**—about **$22 in federal income tax savings** at a 22% marginal rate.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** So how do the two choices compare after next year?

**Jordan:** Using the same 22% federal marginal rate, choosing **actual expenses this year** saves you **$11 now**, but you use up the remaining $250 carryforward next year and have nothing left. Choosing **simplified this year** gives up that $11, but saves you **$22 more next year** and leaves **$200** to carry forward.

**Alex:** So I’d come out ahead even if I never use that last $200?

**Jordan:** Yes, if next year plays out as assumed. You’d be **$11 ahead in federal income tax savings across the two years**, before accounting for the wait. The remaining $200 has value only if it increases a deduction you can actually claim later.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if next year’s deduction limit turns out to be only $1,100?

**Jordan:** Then both carryforward balances would get you the same **$1,100 deduction** next year: $850 in current expenses plus $250 from the carryforward. That still beats the $1,000 simplified deduction next year. But if you chose simplified **this year**, you’d have **$300 left** to carry forward; if you chose actual expenses this year, you’d have nothing left.

**Alex:** So the $11 I save now would put actual expenses ahead?

**Jordan:** Yes, through next year. After that, choosing simplified this year could still come out ahead if the remaining $300 produces more than $11 in future federal income tax savings, after accounting for the wait. At the same 22% rate and ignoring the wait, that means it would need to increase a later deduction by **more than $50**.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if that $300 increases my deduction by exactly $50 two years from now?

**Jordan:** At the same 22% federal marginal rate, that saves **$11 two years from now**. If none of the remaining carryforward ever helps, the two choices tie in total dollars, but **actual expenses come out ahead once you account for timing**: $11 today is worth more than $11 two years from now.

**Alex:** How much would I need to deduct in two years to break even?

**Jordan:** At a 5% annual discount rate, you’d need about **$55 in additional deductions** in two years. At 22%, that saves about $12.10 then, worth about $11 today. And “additional” still means above the best deduction you could claim without that carryforward.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** So would an extra $55 deduction two years from now actually put me ahead?

**Jordan:** Just barely not. The exact break-even amount is **$55.125** in additional deductions. At a 22% federal marginal rate, $55 saves $12.10 in two years, which is worth about $10.98 today at a 5% annual discount rate. An extra **$56** would put the simplified method slightly ahead, assuming you can claim it in full and the rest of the carryforward never helps.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** How much ahead would I be with the extra $56 deduction?

**Jordan:** About **17 cents in today’s dollars**. At a 22% federal marginal rate, the $56 deduction saves $12.32 in two years. Discounted at 5% per year, that’s worth about $11.17 today, versus the $11 you’d save now by choosing actual expenses.

**Alex:** Is that enough to base the decision on?

**Jordan:** I’d treat it as a tie. A small change in your tax rate, the timing, or how much of the carryforward you can actually use would matter more than those 17 cents.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If it’s basically a tie, what would you use as a tiebreaker?

**Jordan:** I’d look at paperwork and how likely you are to use more of the carryforward. If you already have the records and don’t expect the remaining balance to help, actual expenses let you take the $11 in federal income tax savings now. If you’d rather skip Form 8829 this year or think more of the carryforward could increase a future deduction, the simplified method is reasonable. Either way, keep the prior Form 8829 and note how much carryforward remains.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I choose simplified this year, what should my carryforward note say?

**Jordan:** In our example: “**$550 in unused actual home-office expenses carried forward. Used the simplified method this year; none of the carryforward was claimed.**” Keep that note with the prior Form 8829 and preserve the breakdown by expense category. If you choose actual expenses instead and use $300 as projected, update the balance to **$250** based on the completed form.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Should I put the tax year on the note?

**Jordan:** Yes. Write: “**Tax year [year], [Schedule C business]: Used the simplified home-office method. Claimed $0 of the prior actual-expense carryforward. Balance at year-end: $550.**” Keep it with the Form 8829 that shows where the balance came from, and copy the expense-category breakdown from that form. The note is for your records; you don’t file it with your return.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** Which year should I put in the heading—the year the $550 came from or the year I used the simplified method?

**Jordan:** Use the **tax year you used the simplified method** in the heading. Then list the source year separately so you can trace the balance back to the right Form 8829. For example: “**Tax year 2026 — simplified method. Prior carryforward: $550 from 2025 Form 8829. Claimed in 2026: $0. Year-end carryforward: $550.**” Keep the expense-category breakdown with that note.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** What if I use the simplified method again in 2027?

**Jordan:** Make a new note for 2027, but keep 2025 as the source year: “**Tax year 2027 — simplified method. Beginning carryforward: $550 from 2025 Form 8829. Claimed in 2027: $0. Year-end carryforward: $550.**” Keep both annual notes with the original Form 8829 and its expense-category breakdown. You don’t file Form 8829 just to track the balance in a simplified-method year.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** If I switch back to actual expenses in 2028, which year’s form do I use?

**Jordan:** Use **Form 8829 for 2028** to calculate that year’s deduction. Use your **2025 Form 8829** to verify the $550 carryforward and its expense-category breakdown. Your 2026 and 2027 notes show that you didn’t claim any of it in those years.

**Alex:** What if I can’t deduct the full $550 in 2028?

**Jordan:** Apply the 2028 deduction limit and use the completed 2028 form to track what remains by expense category. Keep it with the 2025 form and your annual notes so you can trace the balance.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I use actual expenses again in 2029, do I copy the original $550 from my 2025 form?

**Jordan:** No. Use the **carryforward amounts shown on your completed 2028 Form 8829**, by expense category, when you fill out the 2029 form. For example, if you deduct $300 of the original $550 in 2028 and have no newly disallowed expenses, you’d carry **$250** into 2029. If some of your 2028 expenses were also disallowed, the balance could be higher. Keep the 2025 form to document where the original $550 came from.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if I use the simplified method in 2029 instead?

**Jordan:** You wouldn’t claim any of the **$250** in 2029, but you wouldn’t lose it. Note that you used the simplified method and that your year-end carryforward is still $250. Keep that note with your **2028 Form 8829**. The next time you use actual expenses, use the remaining balance by expense category from that form—not the original $550 from 2025.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** If I switch back to actual expenses in 2030, do I need to file a 2029 Form 8829 first?

**Jordan:** No. Use **Form 8829 for 2030** and bring in the **$250 carryforward by expense category** from your completed 2028 form, subject to the 2030 deduction limit. Keep your 2029 note with your records to show why the balance didn’t change. You don’t file a 2029 Form 8829 just to document the carryforward.

speaker: A
text:
**Alex:** What if my qualifying office is a different size in 2030?

**Jordan:** Recalculate the business-use percentage for your **2030 expenses** using the new office and home measurements. Don’t apply that percentage again to the **$250 carryforward**: it’s already a business-use amount. Enter it by expense category on the 2030 Form 8829 and let that year’s deduction limit determine how much you can claim.

speaker: B
text:
**Alex:** Can you show me what that looks like with numbers?

**Jordan:** Say your 2030 office is 120 square feet in a 1,200-square-foot apartment and qualifies all year. Your business-use percentage is **10%**. If you pay $12,000 in eligible rent and utilities, the business share is **$1,200**. Bring in the **full $250 carryforward** by expense category—not 10% of it. That gives you **$1,450 before the deduction limit**, assuming the rules stay the same.

**Alex:** What if I can’t deduct the full $1,450?

**Jordan:** Use the completed 2030 Form 8829 to see what remains eligible to carry forward in each expense category. That becomes the balance you track going forward.
